catalog_quote: Barasa (2012) identifies two register tones for Ateso, high and low. Further analysis on the expanded data used for the present study reveals that, at the phonetic level, four tones occur in Ateso: high, marked with an acute accent (´), low, marked with a grave accent (`), a high tone downstep transcribed with an acute accent followed by an arrow pointing downwards (´ꜜ) and a contour or falling tone, transcribed with a circumflex ( ̂) on the vowel. ... All tones are associated with segmental phonemes. They are contrastively assigned to vowels in all lexical elements, meaning that all vowels carry tone. A vowel carries a single tonal element, H or L, or a sequence of two tonal elements, HL. Tonal configurations can combine freely in words; an alternative sequence of high and low tones is most common, with rare occurrence of falling tones at word ends. ... audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal; no word-stress rule stated) rests on the only modern reference grammar of Ateso (Barasa 2017, Glottolog's MED long_grammar), which we hold with a good text layer; the deciding tone quotation and the p. 233 remark were re-confirmed verbatim at the stated pages, and the secondary Hilders & Lawrance 1956 'equal stress... root syllable perhaps slightly more; stress does not affect pitch or tone' passage was re-confirmed in the held archive.org text. The newer open item fetched sources now (Barasa 2018, ATR harmony) is silent on prosody. Remaining unheld works (Tucker & Bryan 1966, Otaala 1981, Schrock 2014 ms.) are older, narrower or unpublished and could at most add an explicit 'no distinctive stress' sentence; none is likely to change TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT.
